title: Effects of vitamin D supplementation on cardiac biomarkers: Results from the STURDY trial

sections.abstract:
In this ancillary study of a double-blind, randomized, response-adaptive trial that tested the effects of 4 doses of vitamin D3 supplementation, there were no significant changes in hs-cTnI and NT-proBNP over time at 3 months, 12 months, or 24 months between dose assignments.

There is an inverse association between vitamin D level and hs-cTnI. Nevertheless, higher supplementation of vitamin D3 does not improve hs-cTnI changes over time.

These findings do not support use of higher doses of vitamin D3 to prevent CVD events.

Keywords: Vitamin D, Cardiac Biomarkers, Preventative Cardiology, Cardiac Injury, Cardiac Strain, Troponin, pro-BNP, Vitamin D Supplementation
sections.introduction:
Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the primary cause of death among adults over age 65 years [ 1 ]. Low blood levels of vitamin D are common among older adults and strongly associated with CVD across multiple observational studies [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] ]. There are well-delineated biologic mechanisms demonstrating that vitamin D reduces hypertrophic signaling in cardiovascular tissue and vascular endothelial cells [ 6 ]. Moreover, vitamin D has been shown to regulate vascular tone and prevent cardiac fibrosis [ 3 ]. Nevertheless, trials of vitamin D supplementation have not found any benefit from vitamin D supplementation on CVD risk, including the recent VITAL trial of 20,000 adults [ 7 ]. Moreover, in the WHI CaD trial where post-menopausal women were randomly assigned to calcium-vitamin D supplementation versus placebo, there was also an increase in CVD mortality among participants receiving supplementation over more than 20 years of follow-up [ 8 ]. However, many of these trials tested lower doses of vitamin D supplementation (400 IU to 1100 IU) among adults that were not required to have a vitamin D insufficiency [ [9] , [10] , [11] , [12] ]. Moreover, CVD outcomes may be too far downstream from the subclinical effects of vitamin D deficiency to observe an impact from supplementation on CVD events in short-term, clinical trials.

Cardiac biomarkers including high-sensitivity cardiac troponin level (hs-cTnI) and N-terminal pro-b-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) are effective means of characterizing subclinical CVD [ 13 ]. Increases in cardiac troponin are associated with myocardial injury [ 14 ] and increases in NT-proBNP are associated with myocardial strain [ 15 ]. A rise in either of these markers over time are associated with incident CVD [ [16] , [17] , [18] , [19] , [20] ]. Moreover, both hs-cTnI and NT-proBNP are associated with vitamin D deficiency in observational studies [ 21 ], and respond to short-term lifestyle interventions [ 22 ]. Thus, these biomarkers can be used to evaluate the effects of vitamin D on two distinct pathways of subclinical cardiovascular injury.

The Study to Understand Fall Reduction and Vitamin D in You (STURDY) was a double-blind, randomized, response-adaptive trial that sought to determine the effects of four doses of vitamin D3 (200, 1000, 2000, and 4000 IU/day) on fall risk in older adults ages 70 years or older with low serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D] levels between 10–29 ng/mL. Ultimately, higher doses of vitamin D3 supplements (i.e., 1000, 2000, or 4000 IU/day) did not lower the risk of falls over up to 2 years of follow-up. However, whether supplementation reduced subclinical CVD was not evaluated during the study.

In this post-hoc analysis, we sought to evaluate the effect of higher dose vitamin D3 supplementation (1000+ IU/day) compared to 200 IU/day on hs-cTnI and NT-proBNP, representing two distinct pathways of subclinical cardiac injury. We hypothesized that 25(OH)D levels would be inversely associated with hs-cTnI and NT-proBNP and that supplementation with higher doses of vitamin D3 would lower the levels of these cardiac biomarkers.
sections.methods:
STURDY was a National Institute of Aging (NIA)-sponsored trial conducted at two community-based research institutions between July 2015 and March 2019. The trial's design, main findings, and protocol have already been published [ 23 ]. The Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center ceded review to the Johns Hopkins University Institutional Review Board, who approved the core study and cardiac biomarkers proposal. All participants provided written, informed consent.

STURDY enrolled adults living in surrounding communities, ages 70 or older with an elevated fall risk (i.e., 2 or more falls or 1 injurious fall in the past year, fear of falling, difficulty maintaining balance, or use of an assistive device), who had a low serum 25(OH)D level (between 10–29 ng/mL). STURDY excluded adults with cognitive impairment, hypercalcemia, and kidney stones. If participants consumed ≤1000 IU/day of vitamin D3 supplements or ≤1200 mg/day of calcium supplements, they remained eligible as long as they met the other trial criteria.

Participants were followed up to 24 months or until study termination. Primary study endpoints were time-to-first fall or death. Participants were followed even after fall events. Study visits occurred at baseline, 3 months, 12 months, and 24 months.

STURDY was a response-adaptive trial. In the dose-finding phase, participants were randomized to one of four doses of vitamin D3 supplementation: 200, 1000, 2000, or 4000 IU/day, with 200 IU/day as the reference dose. The probability of assignment to 200 IU/day was 0.50 throughout the duration of the trial. The starting probability of assignment to the non-control doses (1000, 2000, 4000 IU/day) was 0.1667. Assignment probabilities to the non-control doses were adjusted using Bayes’ Theorem at pre-specified times after the 100th participant was randomized to the non-control group.

In the dose-finding phase, STURDY found that the 1000 IU/day dose was the best non-control dose for preventing falls. At this point, in the confirmatory phase, all active participants assigned to the other non-control doses (i.e., 2000 or 4000 IU/day) were transitioned to the 1000 IU/day dose, and newly enrolled participants were randomly assigned to either 200 IU/day or 1000 IU/day at a 0.50 probability of assignment. The combined group of participants initially assigned to 1000 IU/day or later transitioned to 1000 IU/day is collectively referred to as 1000+ IU/day in this study. Randomization in the dose-finding stage began October 30, 2015, and ended March 23, 2018. The confirmatory stage began April 10, 2018, and ended May 31, 2019.

As previously described, the proportion of participants who reported taking their study pill at least 80 % of the expected days was 72.5 % in the 200 IU/day group and 75.8 % in the 1000+ IU/day group. At 3 months after randomization, the mean 25(OH)D was 27.0 ng/mL among those assigned 200 IU/day versus 36.4 ng/mL among those assigned 1000+ IU/day.

Cardiac biomarkers used for the present analysis (hs-cTnI and NT-proBNP) were measured at University of Maryland in 2022 from stored serum specimens, collected at baseline, 3-month, 12-month, and 24-month visits. The biomarkers were selected based on their relationship with two distinct pathways of subclinical cardiac damage: subclinical myocyte injury (hs-cTnI) and cardiac strain as a marker of wall stress (NT-proBNP) as well as their ability to predict CVD events in adults without known CVD [ [16] , [17] , [18] , [19] , [20] ].

Non-fasting serum specimens were collected from participants. All serum had been stored at -70 °C and underwent at least one freeze-thaw cycle prior to the present measurements. There were 673 specimens available at baseline (98 % of 688), 626 at 3-months (97 % of 643; note there were only 625 NT-proBNP at the 3-month visit), 505 at 12 months (97 % of 521), and 323 at 24 months (95 % of 339). Missing data were evenly distributed across supplement assignments ( Supplement Figure SF1 ).

Measurement kits and assays were donated by Siemens (Siemens Healthineers, Malvern, Pennsylvania) for: (1) ADVIA Centaur High-Sensitivity Troponin I (reported within-run CV of 4.8 % for a mean of 13.11 ng/L [or pg/mL]), and (2) Dimension Vista N-terminal Pro-Brain Natriuretic Peptide (reported within-run CV of 1.4 % for a mean of 120 pg/mL). Biomarker assays had the following limits of detection: <1.60 ng/L (hs-cTnI) and <5 pg/mL (NT-proBNP). Given the larger number of hs-cTnI values below the limit of detection, we also examined an alternate measurement cut point based on the assay's the limit of blank (<0.5 ng/L) in sensitivity analyses. Notably, the limit of detection is the manufacturer's lowest concentration of hs-cTnI that can be detected with 95 % probability, while the limit of blank is the highest measurement that might be observed for a blank sample. For hs-cTnI, we imputed zero values of hs-cTnI (N=6), using the lowest reported concentration (0.21 ng/dL) divided by the sqrt(2) [ 24 ].

Participants reported age, sex, and race. Race was included in the analysis given the role of skin absorption of ultraviolet light in the synthesis of active form of vitamin D [ 25 , 26 ]. Body mass index (BMI, kg/m 2 ) was calculated based on measured height and weight. Participants were also asked (yes or no) about their history of CVD, diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, kidney disease or reduced kidney function and a fall event in the past year. Participants’ baseline 25(OH)D levels were grouped into categories of 10–14 ng/mL, 15–19 ng/mL, 20–24 ng/mL, and 25–29 ng/mL, and dichotomously as 10–19 ng/mL or 20–29 ng/mL. Participant frailty was determined as robust, pre-frail, or frail based on definitions described elsewhere [ 23 ]. Seated systolic and diastolic blood pressure (mmHg) were measured after a 5-minute rest as the average of 3 measurements resulting from an OMRON HEM-907XL oscillometric device.

Baseline characteristics were summarized using means (SD) and proportions.

The serum biomarkers were log-transformed to address data skew. We used tobit models to determine the cross-sectional association between categories of baseline 25(OH)D and relative %-difference in hs-cTnI or NT-proBNP. Tobit models permit informative left-censoring, observed below the limit of detection (or blank) for each assay. This feature makes it possible to use a linear regression model in the detectable range and designate undetectable biomarkers as below the detectable range [ 27 ]. All models used the assays’ limits of detection to specify the bound between detectable and undetectable values. For hs-cTnI, we also examined the limit of blank in sensitivity analyses. Models were unadjusted; adjusted for age, sex, and Black race (Model 1); and adjusted for age, sex, Black race, seated systolic blood pressure, seated diastolic blood pressure, BMI, history of CVD, history of diabetes, history of high blood pressure, and history of a fall in the past year (Model 2).

Like the original STURDY trial, in this ancillary study, the primary comparison was between those assigned to higher vitamin D3 doses (1000+ IU/day) and those assigned to the lower vitamin D3 dose (200 IU/day). We determined the geometric means of serum concentrations of the log-transformed biomarkers using mixed effects tobit models (metobit command). The fixed portion of the tobit model included supplement assignment (with values 0 [200 IU/day] or 1 [1000+ IU/day]), a visit variable (values 0 [baseline] or 1 [the 3-, 12-, 24-month visit], corresponding to baseline and each of the in-person visits with phlebotomy), and the interaction of these terms. The random effects portion of the tobit model included participant identification number, which introduced a random intercept. We determined both absolute and relative changes from baseline and the difference between these changes across assignments.

Trend analyses were performed using similar models by treating the visit variable as a categorical variable with values of 0, 3, 12, and 24, corresponding to baseline and each of the in-person visits with phlebotomy, spaced approximately 3, 12, and 24 months after randomization. Trends were examined by subsequently treating the visit variable above as a continuous variable. In sensitivity analyses, models were repeated comparing each individual vitamin D supplementation dose with follow-up censored at the end of the dose-finding stage.

Models were repeated in strata of age (<80 years, ≥80 years), female sex (no, yes), Black race (no, yes), history of CVD (no, yes), history of diabetes (no, yes), history of high blood pressure or hypertension (no, yes), fall in the past year (no, yes), history of hyperlipidemia, history of kidney disease, frailty, or baseline 25OHD level (10–19 ng/mL or 20–29 ng/mL). Comparisons across strata were based on three-way interaction terms (treatment-by-visit-by-stratification variable).

We considered a two-tailed P -value <0.05 statistically significant. Analyses were performed with Stata version 15.1 (Stata Corporation, College Station, TX, USA).
sections.results:
Baseline characteristics of the STURDY trial participants by vitamin D supplementation are shown in Table 1 . The mean age was 76.5 (SD, 5.4) years with 43.6 % women and 18.2 % Black adults. There were 29.4 % of participants with a history of CVD. The average 25(OH)D level was 22.1 ng/mL. Notably, there was a greater skew toward ages ≥ 80 yrs (28.9 %) and a higher proportion of CVD history (31.3 %) in the 200-IU/day dose group, and a higher proportion of women (45.6 %), Black adults (19.9 %), and adults with history of hypertension (66.2 %) and hyperlipidemia (57.3 %) among the 1000-IU/day dose group. There were 677 unique persons with hs-cTnI values, and 676 unique persons for NT-proBNP values.

Baseline characteristics by Dose of vitamin D supplementation.

Black race was unknown for 4 participants assigned to the 200 IU/day group and 3 participants assigned the 1000+ IU/day group.

There were only 348 with blood pressure, body mass index, and frailty measures in the 1000+ IU/day group.

In the fully adjusted model, baseline serum 25(OH)D categories (i.e., 10–19 and 20–29 ng/mL) were not associated with baseline hs-cTnI. When treated as a continuous variable, every 1 ng/mL-higher level of 25(OH)D was associated with a lower hs-cTnI, even after adjustment (-1.7 %-difference; 95 % CI: -3.1, -0.4) ( Supplement Table ST3 ). In contrast, there was no association between baseline 25(OH)D levels and NT-proBNP.

Mean baseline concentrations of hs-cTnI and NT-proBNP were similar between 200 IU/day and 1000+ IU/day vitamin D supplementation assignments ( Table 2 ). While not statistically significant, it appeared hs-cTnI increased more from baseline in the higher-dose group (7.0 % in higher vs. 5.2 % in lower), while the NT-proBNP increased more in the lower-dose group (9.3 % in higher vs. 11.3 % in lower). There was no statistically significant between-group difference. Also when evaluating the effect of individual doses (200 IU/day, 1000 IU/day, 2000 IU/day, 4000 IU/day) of vitamin D supplementation, there was no statistically significant difference in the change in baseline or between-groups ( Supplemental Table ST4).

sections.discussion:
In this population of older adults with low levels of serum vitamin D, we examined the effect of higher doses of vitamin D supplementation on two markers of subclinical cardiac injury and strain. While there was a suggestion that higher vitamin D levels were associated with lower hs-cTnI, higher doses of vitamin D supplementation did not reduce hs-cTnI. Similarly, neither baseline serum vitamin D levels nor higher dose supplementation impacted NT-proBNP. Findings were largely consistent regardless of demographic or baseline comorbid conditions. These findings do not support the use of higher dose vitamin D supplementation to reduce CVD risk in adults with low blood levels of vitamin D.

Multiple observational studies have demonstrated an inverse relationship between vitamin D and CVD [ [28] , [29] , [30] ]. Moreover, several meta-analyses of vitamin D3 trials have suggested that supplementation may lower blood pressure, [ 31 , 32 ] a CVD risk factor, particularly at doses >800 IU/day [ 33 ] and reduce the risk of all-cause and CVD mortality [ 34 ]. Recent studies have tested the effect of vitamin D supplementation on cardiac biomarkers with mixed results. Zebrowska et al found that three weeks of 800 IU/day vitamin D supplementation in competitive runners decreased immediate and 1 hr-post-exercise troponin levels [ 35 ]. Similarly, El-Bassinouy et al found that 20 IU/day vitamin D supplementation in breast cancer patients receiving adjuvant doxorubicin chemotherapy reduced cardiac troponin levels compared to baseline after 4 cycles of chemotherapy [ 36 ]. However, in a post-hoc analysis of cardiac biomarkers by Wu et al with older adults receiving monthly 100,000 IU vitamin D, there was no significant relative difference in geometric means of hs-cTnI and NT-proBNP between vitamin D and placebo groups [ 37 ]. Similarly, in an analysis of type 2 diabetes patients by Limonte et al, compared with placebo, vitamin supplementation with 2000 IU/day did not significantly reduce NT-proBNP over 5 years [ 38 ]. This evidence has led to mixed beliefs that appropriately dosed vitamin D might prevent CVD events. However, trials to support this hypothesis, and translation into clinical practice has been limited by: (1) designs where CVD was not the primary outcome [ 31 , 32 , 39 ], (2) administration of non-physiologic doses of vitamin D3 (e.g., periodic high-dose injections rather than daily dosing) [ 37 , 40 ], and (3) inclusion of participants with normal (versus low) blood levels of vitamin D [ 36 , 41 , 42 ]. Furthermore, many trials enrolled predominantly younger adults. The present study addresses many of these limitations by examining the effects of higher versus lower doses of daily vitamin D supplementation among an older, vitamin D insufficient population.

There are few randomized controlled trials to date evaluating the role of vitamin D supplementation on CVD as the primary outcome. The VITamin D and OmegA-3 TriaL (VITAL) was a large-scale randomized placebo-controlled trial of daily supplementation in the primary prevention of cancer and CVD [ 7 ]. In this trial, major CVD events were a composite of MI, stroke, and CVD mortality. Vitamin D did not reduce major CVD events [ 7 ]. There are limitations to the VITAL trial, which our analysis addresses. First, in VITAL the observed lack of benefit of vitamin D supplementation only reflected a single dose of vitamin D compared to placebo. Our trial compared both high and low dose supplementation, and further supports that regardless of dose, vitamin D supplementation did not impact subclinical cardiac injury. The VITAL trial also did not identify adults as having low serum vitamin D levels, a selection criterion for STURDY. Finally, the VITAL trial focused on cardiovascular outcomes including myocardial infarction, stroke, and mortality, which may be too far removed from the pathological process of low vitamin D to see a strong effect even over several years. Our study focused on sensitive markers of cardiac injury, hs-cTnI and NT-proBNP, which are strongly associated with higher risk of CVD events long-term [ 19 , 21 ]. These biomarkers are highly sensitive, and may more accurately reflect the short-term effects of vitamin D supplementation on cardiac injury pathways.

Low serum vitamin D has been linked with heart strain [ 43 ]. One meta-analysis found that vitamin D3 strongly prevented future heart failure, but not ischemic events in older adults [ 41 ]. In addition, this low serum vitamin D in patients with chronic heart failure has been shown to be associated with poor prognosis [ 44 ]. Moreover, vitamin D administration has been shown to have a positive effect on ventricular remodeling, left ventricle end-diastolic diameter, and left ventricular ejection fraction [ 45 ]. However, our study showed similar changes in NT-proBNP over time regardless of lower or higher vitamin D doses. Interestingly, the higher dose of vitamin D supplementation did result in greater reductions of NT-proBNP among adults age 80 years and older. This observation is reflected in the work of Wu et al where among patients with low serum vitamin D levels, follow-up NT-proBNP at one or two years was significantly lower in the monthly vitamin D group compared to placebo [ 37 ]. Reasons for this observation are unclear. We can speculate that the systemic effects of vitamin D deficiency are more profound amongst the very old, and there may be an inverse relationship between supplementation and inflammation. It is also possible that serum vitamin D level is a risk marker but not a risk factor for CVD risk and related underlying mechanisms. This observation may also reflect a false positive due to multiple testing. Additional work is needed to replicate these findings.

Our study has limitations. First, STURDY was a community-based population. While a number had elevated CVD risk factors, baseline cardiac biomarkers were lower than some populations at high risk for CVD events. Moreover, our results may not be generalizable to populations at higher risk of CVD. As a result, it is possible that assay performance may be less precise or already too low to determine benefit. Second, in two hypertension trials, blood pressure-lowering interventions that reduced the risk of CVD events did not impact troponin levels [ 46 , 47 ]; these studies suggest that troponin levels may not be an appropriate marker for the effect of vitamin D on CVD. Third, we may not have had adequate power for our cross-sectional analyses as well as subgroup analyses. Fourth, both groups received some vitamin D3 supplementation. As a result, we are unable to determine the impact of lower dose supplementation versus no supplementation among our population. Fifth, while our cardiac biomarkers are quite sensitive for subclinical CVD and predictive of future events, they are still merely surrogates for the CVD outcomes of interest. Sixth, low vitamin D may be a risk marker that co-associates with other risk factors that affect CVD, and therefore vitamin D supplementation is of a little benefit in this population if other risk factors are not controlled. Finally, while participants were asked about kidney disease it was not measured at baseline. As a result, it is possible some cases of chronic kidney disease were missed.

Our study also has a number of strengths. First, the vitamin D3 supplementation doses were tightly controlled and administered in a randomized fashion. Second, there was high adherence and follow-up rates for both lower and higher doses of vitamin D3. This allowed us to evaluate the role of vitamin D3 dose on cardiac biomarkers. Third, our markers of subclinical CVD are highly sensitive and strongly predictive of CVD events [ [16] , [17] , [18] , [19] , [20] ]. Moreover, they have been shown to be responsive to short-term dietary intervention studies [ 22 ]. Finally, we enrolled an older population with vitamin D insufficiency or deficiency, which is a group thought to be well-positioned to benefit from supplementation.

Our study has potential clinical implications. Vitamin D deficiency is one of the most common vitamin deficiencies worldwide [ 48 , 49 ], and CVD is the leading cause of death in the United States [ 50 ]. Vitamin D deficiency has been associated with endothelial dysfunction, ventricular hypertrophy, and cardiac tissue cell regulation in animal experimental and human observational studies [ 6 , 51 , 52 ]. In our study, at baseline there was an inverse association between vitamin D level and hs-cTnI. Nevertheless, higher supplementation did not improve hs-cTnI changes over time. Moreover, there were no significant changes in hs-cTnI and NT-proBNP over time at 3 months, 12 months, or 24 months between dose assignments. This study strongly illustrates that cross-sectional relationships should not be construed as causal. While much work is needed to understand why vitamin D deficiency is associated with CVD, our study adds to the growing body of evidence that daily or monthly supplementation with vitamin D does not prevent CVD events [ 7 ] or reduce or reduce markers of subclinical cardiac injury or strain. [ 37 , 38 ] Instead, there may be other factors upstream to vitamin D and CVD (e.g., outdoor physical activity, general health) that may be a better target for preventive interventions.

In conclusion, in this population of older adults with vitamin D deficiency, a higher dose of vitamin D3 supplementation did not reduce markers of subclinical cardiac disease. These findings do not support use of higher doses of vitamin D3 to prevent CVD events.
